Add a new heading ## Quality filtering with fastp to notes.md, and below it:

The command that made samples.txt, and the check
The sbatch command with a comment that names the script, and below the code block, the job ID
The checks on the output: what you expected and what you saw
The scp command that copied the reports to your computer (remember: # On my computer)
Below the code block, in your own words: what did the fastp report show for Sample-DUMMY1? How many reads were there before and after filtering? Did anything surprise you?

The test run on one sample was a detour, so you don’t need its commands. One sentence on what it taught you is enough, for example that fastp writes its reports to fastp.html and fastp.json unless you give other names.









TipTip: Comparing reads before and after trimming (optional)





At the start of the day, we made a table with seqkit stats for the raw reads. If we make the same table for the trimmed reads, we can see what fastp changed:

# Run seqkit stats on the trimmed reads
srun --cpus-per-task=1 --mem=5G --time=00:30:00 seqkit stats -b -a -T -o results/seqkit/stats_trimmed.txt results/fastp/*trimmed.fastq.gz --threads 1

# Check the output: we expect a header line and 8 lines, one per trimmed file
wc -l results/seqkit/stats_trimmed.txt
cat results/seqkit/stats_trimmed.txt

Both tables have many columns, which makes them hard to compare by eye. On day 1, we used cut to select columns. Here, we use awk, a small programming language for working with tables in text files. awk reads a file line by line, splits each line into columns, and lets us choose what to do with each line.
Let’s print the file name, the number of reads and the average read length (columns 1, 4 and 7) of both tables:

awk -F'\t' 'FNR > 1 {print $1, $4, $7}' results/seqkit/stats_raw.txt results/seqkit/stats_trimmed.txt

Here:

-F'\t': the columns are separated by tabs (\t stands for a tab)
'...': the awk program, in single quotes so that bash does not change anything in it
FNR > 1: only work on lines with a line number above 1. This skips the header line. FNR is the line number within the current file, so the header is skipped in both files
{print $1, $4, $7}: print columns 1, 4 and 7. In awk, $4 means “column 4”. This is not the same as a bash variable
We give awk two files, and it works through them one after the other

This prints 16 lines: first the 8 raw files, then the 8 trimmed files. Compare the number of reads and the average length of Sample-DUMMY1 before and after trimming.









TipTip: Finding R2 without a list file (optional)





For those who want to learn more bash: we can also write this loop without samples.txt. We then loop directly over the R1 files, and let bash work out the matching R2 file and the sample name:

for R1 in data/seq_project/*/*_R1.fastq.gz; do
    R2=${R1/_R1/_R2}
    sample=$(basename $R1 _R1.fastq.gz)
    echo "Sample: $sample, R1: $R1, R2: $R2"
done


${R1/_R1/_R2}: takes the value of R1 and replaces the first _R1 with _R2. This turns the path to the R1 file into the path to the R2 file
basename $R1 _R1.fastq.gz: basename removes the folders from a path and keeps only the file name. If you give it an ending as second argument, it removes that ending too. What is left is the sample name
$( ): the command substitution from above stores the output of basename in the variable sample

This is shorter, but you need to know the extra syntax to read it. A list file is easier to check, and easier to change if you want to run only some samples.
If your list file has several columns, for example a sample name and a group, a while loop can read both columns into separate variables. The IBED for-loops page explains this, and builds a loop step by step with another example.

title: Using an HPC
text:
Wrapping up day 2
Your analysis now lives in two places: the data, results and job scripts on Crunchomics, and the notebook on your own computer. The notebook mentions the job scripts, so let’s copy them next to it. Run this in the terminal on your own computer:

# Run this on your OWN computer, inside your local data_analysis folder
# Replace both instances of 'username' with your UvAnetID
scp 'username@omics-h0.science.uva.nl:/home/username/personal/data_analysis/scripts/*.sh' scripts/

# Check: we expect count_lines.sh from day 1, and seqkit.sh and fastp.sh from today
ls -l scripts

As in the fastp exercise, the quotes around the path stop your own computer from using the wildcard, so that Crunchomics can use it to find the files.






NotebookNotebook checkpoint: Tidy your notebook (day 2)






Add the scp command that copied the scripts to your notebook
Update the description at the top of notes.md, so that it covers both days
Check that your notebook explains every file and folder in your project on Crunchomics. Run these inside ~/personal/data_analysis: ls, ls results/* and ls scripts logs. Can you tell which log file belongs to which job?
Compare your notebook with my example notebook. What does it have that yours doesn’t? Is there anything you want to add?

title: Using an HPC
text:
Going further






TipTip: Running many files in parallel with job arrays (optional)





Our fastp loop runs inside a single job, so the samples are processed one after another. With 4 small samples, that is fine. With hundreds of samples, it can take a long time, while the HPC has enough space to run several of them at the same time.
For this section, we go back to seqkit stats and run it on each file separately, one job per file. How would we run such jobs efficiently?
We can use a job array, which allows us to:

Run several jobs with the same settings: the same CPUs, memory and software
Run these jobs in parallel (at the same time), instead of one after the other

Let’s start with making a list of the files we want to work with, using what we learned on day 1:

ls data/seq_project/*/*.gz | cut -f4 -d "/" > fastq_files.txt

# Check the list: we expect 8 file names
cat fastq_files.txt
wc -l fastq_files.txt

Next, we use this text file in our job array. Store the following in scripts/array.sh:

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=my_array
#SBATCH --output=logs/array_%A_%a.out
#SBATCH --error=logs/array_%A_%a.err
#SBATCH --array=1-8
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1
#SBATCH --mem=5G

# The number of the current job in the array (1 to 8 for our 8 files)
index=$SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID

# Read the file name on line number $index of fastq_files.txt
current_sample=$(sed -n "${index}p" fastq_files.txt)

# Print what is happening
echo "Now Job${index} runs on ${current_sample}"

# Run the actual job
seqkit stats -b -a -T -o results/seqkit/${current_sample}_stats.txt data/seq_project/*/${current_sample} --threads 1

In the script, we use some new SLURM options:

#SBATCH --array=1-8: sets up a job array with 8 jobs, numbered 1 to 8. We choose 1-8 because we have exactly 8 fastq.gz files
#SBATCH --output=logs/array_%A_%a.out: %A is replaced by the job ID that SLURM assigns, and %a by the number of the job in the array
Important: do the individual jobs in your array use a lot of CPUs or memory? Then you might not want to run all of them at the same time. With #SBATCH --array=1-8%2, SLURM runs at most 2 jobs at the same time, and starts the next ones when these have finished. Try to use no more than ~20% of the Crunchomics cluster at the same time.

The script does the following:

index stores the value of SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID, the number of the current job within the array. This is 1 for the first job, 2 for the second, …, and 8 for the last one
sed -n "${index}p" fastq_files.txt prints one line of fastq_files.txt: line 1 for job 1, line 2 for job 2, and so on. We store this file name in the variable current_sample. For the first job, this is Sample-DUMMY1_R1.fastq.gz
echo records which job works on which file
Finally, we run seqkit stats on the file stored in current_sample. Each job writes its own table, named after its input file, so the 8 jobs don’t overwrite each other’s output

Submit the script with sbatch scripts/array.sh. If we check what is happening right after submitting the job with squeue, we should see something like this:





We see that jobs 1-4 are already running, and jobs 5-8 are waiting for space. That is one of the useful things about a job manager such as SLURM: it finds the resources on all nodes for us, as long as we requested sensible amounts of CPUs and memory.
If we check the log files, we should see something like this:





We get an output and an error file for each job. In the output, we see the value stored in index, here 1, and in current_sample, here Sample-DUMMY1_R1.fastq.gz.
Check that each job wrote its table:

# We expect 8 tables, one per fastq.gz file
ls -l results/seqkit/*_stats.txt
ls results/seqkit/*_stats.txt | wc -l

More about arrays and other SLURM options can be found on the IBED SLURM basics page.

title: Introduction to Bash
section: pwd: Find out where we are
text:
pwd: Find out where we are
To get started, open your terminal and get yourself oriented by typing your first command, pwd, and then pressing enter:

pwd

The command pwd stands for print working directory. The working directory is the folder your shell is operating on right now, so pwd tells you where you currently are in the file system. You should see something like this:
/Users/YourUserName
When you open a new terminal, you start in what is called your home directory. This is your personal folder on the computer.
What the path to your home directory looks like depends on your system:

Mac: /Users/YourUserName
MobaXterm (Windows): /home/mobaxterm
WSL2 (Windows) and Linux: /home/YourUserName

In this tutorial, we work inside the home directory. That way, the commands are the same for everybody.

title: Introduction to Bash
section: ls: List the contents of a directory
text:
ls: List the contents of a directory
Now that you know where you are, let’s find out what is inside it: which files and folders are there. The command ls (short for list) shows the files and folders in your current directory. Type the following and press enter:

ls

In my case this returns something like this (and this will look different for your current directory):



The colors and formatting depend on your terminal settings, but typically:

Folders (directories) appear in one color (in my example above: green)
Files appear in another (in my example above: bold white)

If your directory contains many items, the output can quickly become overwhelming. To make sense of it, we can use options and arguments to control how commands behave.

title: Introduction to Bash
text:
The structure of a command
A command generally has three parts:

A command name: the program you want to run, e.g. ls
An option (or flag): a way to change how the command behaves, e.g. -l changes the output from ls from long to list format. Options usually start with a -
An argument: the input the command works on, e.g. a file or folder. Some commands work without an argument




Try the following command in your current directory to list (ls) the contents of the current folder and show details in long format (-l)“:

ls -l

After running this, we see our files and folders again but as a more detailed list. In the example below you can now see additional information about who is allowed to read and change the files (the access modes), who owns them, how large the files are, when they were last modified and of course their name:









TipTip: Using ls in practice





Throughout this tutorial, you’ll notice that we use ls a lot. There is a reason for that.
When working with data, sanity checks are essential, because it is easy to make mistakes, overwrite files, or lose track of where things are. Simple commands like ls, pwd, wc or grep help you check what is happening to your files at every step of an analysis.
These habits are not just for beginners, bioinformaticians rely on them constantly.

title: Introduction to Bash
text:
Getting help
At some point, you’ll want to know what options a command has or how it works. In this case, first check if a manual page (or man page) is available for the command by typing man followed by the command name:

man ls

This opens the manual entry for the command ls. You can move through it using:

the ↑ / ↓ arrow keys, or the space bar to move down one page
b to move back up one page
q to quit the manual

Not all programs come with such a manual. Depending on the program, there are a few common ways to get help that you can try:

man ls
ls --help
ls -h

title: Introduction to Bash
text:
mkdir: Make new folders
Before we start moving around, let’s first learn how to create new folders (also called directories). This is something we will do often, for example to keep raw data, results and scripts organized in separate places. The command we use for that is mkdir, which stands for make directory.
We use mkdir to create a project folder called data_analysis for this tutorial. Don’t worry about the cd ~ in the first line yet, we cover moving around in the next section. For now, it is enough to know that it takes you to your home directory.

# Move into the home directory
cd ~

# Create a new folder called data_analysis
mkdir data_analysis

# Check that the folder was created
ls

You should see a new folder called data_analysis in the list. We will use this folder as our project folder for all exercises in this tutorial.
You can also look at the same folder in the file browser you know from Windows or Mac. The command below opens the folder you are in right now. The dot (.) is short for “the current folder”:

# Windows (MobaXterm or WSL2): open the current folder in File Explorer
explorer.exe .

# Mac: open the current folder in Finder
open .

Use the command for your own system. You should see a window with your home directory and the new data_analysis folder in it. This is useful later, for example to open a report that you made with the command line.






ImportantMobaXterm users: did you choose a permanent folder?





If explorer.exe . opens a folder in a temporary location, MobaXterm deletes your work when you close it. You can see this in the address bar of File Explorer: it shows Temp, for example Local > Temp > Mxt265 > mx86_64b > tmp > home_YourUserName. Before you continue, follow the steps in MobaXterm: choose a permanent folder on the “Before you start” page. Then make the data_analysis folder again.



Next, let’s make a data folder inside the new data_analysis folder:

# Make a data folder inside the data_analysis folder
# The -p option also makes the parent folder (here: data_analysis) if it does not exist yet
mkdir -p data_analysis/data

# Check that the folder was created
# Notice how we use ls with an option (-l) and an argument (data_analysis)?
ls -l data_analysis







TipTip: Commenting your code





Notice how I added a # and some notes above each command?
Anything written after a # in bash is a comment. A comment is not executed, but it helps you (and others) understand what the code does.
In your own work, add short, meaningful comments above key steps. Avoid restating the obvious. Instead, explain why you do something or what it achieves. A good rule: add a comment wherever you think that future you might get confused a month later.

title: Introduction to Bash
text:
touch: Starting your notebook
Now that we have a project folder, it gets a notebook: a file in which you write down the commands you ran, a comment on what each one does, and a few words about what you saw. Think of it as the lab book of your analysis. Writing it while you work takes a bit of time, but it also makes you stop and think about what you just did. And a month from now, it tells you exactly how you got your results.
We create an empty file for the notebook with touch:

# Create an empty file called notes.md inside the data_analysis folder
touch data_analysis/notes.md

# Check that the file was created: it has a size of 0, because it is still empty
ls -l data_analysis

touch creates an empty file if it does not exist yet. If the file already exists, touch leaves its content alone, so you can not lose your notes by running it twice.
To open the notebook, go to the File Explorer (Windows) or Finder (Mac) window that you opened before, double-click the data_analysis folder and then double-click notes.md. If it opens in a program other than your text editor, right-click the file, choose Open with and pick your editor (for example RStudio). 






TipTip: RStudio users, stay in Source mode





RStudio shows two buttons at the top left of a Markdown file: Source and Visual. Stay in Source. Then you see exactly what you type, including the # and the backticks.




Writing the notebook in Markdown
The file ends in .md because we write it in Markdown: plain text with a few symbols that give it structure. For your notebook, you only need three of them:

A line that starts with # and a space is a heading. More # symbols make a smaller heading (##, ###).
Code goes into a code block: a line with three backticks and the word bash above the code, and a line with three backticks below it. You can replace bash with other language names, like python or r, based on whatever coding language you use for a task.
Everything else is normal text, for example what you saw or why you did something.

Notice that a # means something different in the two places: in normal Markdown text, it starts a heading. Inside a code block, it is a bash comment.
A first entry in your notebook could look like this:
# Notes: Introduction to the command line

## Setting up the project folder

I made a project folder for this workshop in my home directory.

```bash
# Go to the home directory and make the project folder with a data folder inside
cd ~
mkdir data_analysis
mkdir -p data_analysis/data

# Make the notebook
touch data_analysis/notes.md
```
Markdown can do more, for example lists, links and tables. You don’t need these for the workshop, but if you are curious, Markdown Basics on the Quarto website gives an overview.
From now on, you find a blue notebook box at the end of each part of the tutorial. It tells you what to add to your notebook. For the first few, you can compare your notes with mine. Your notes do not have to look the same as mine, as long as future you understands them.

title: Introduction to Bash
text:
cd: Move around folders
Now that we have our own project folder and know how to document what we are doing, let’s learn how to move around the file system with cd (short for change directory).
The file system is structured like a tree that starts from a single root directory, written as a forward slash (/). All other folders branch out from this root directory. For example, we can go from the root directory to the home folder, and from there into the folder with your user name: /home/username.



On your own computer, the start of this path can look different, for example /Users/username on a Mac. Use pwd to see yours.
The location of a file or folder is written as a path: the folder names along the way, separated by /. There are two ways to write a path, for example to the data folder:

An absolute path starts from the root, e.g. cd /home/username/data_analysis/data
A relative path starts from your current location, e.g. cd data if you are already in /home/username/data_analysis

It is generally recommended to use relative paths from inside your project folder. That makes your code more portable: it still works if you move the project folder or run it on another computer.
Let’s practice moving between folders. At each step, use pwd if you feel that you get lost:

# Move into the data_analysis folder
cd data_analysis

# Check where you are
pwd

You now should see something like /Users/YourUserName/data_analysis. You can use cd in multiple ways to move around:

# Move into the data folder
cd data

# Move one level up (..), back to the data_analysis folder
cd ..

# Quickly go back home (you now should be in the home directory)
cd ~

# Move multiple levels down at once
cd data_analysis/data

# Move two levels up, back into the home directory
cd ../..

# And go back to the data_analysis folder
cd data_analysis

In the code above, the tilde symbol (~) is a shortcut for your home directory. It is the same as typing the full absolute path to your home (e.g. cd /Users/YourUserName), but much faster to type. Two dots (..) always mean “the folder one level up”.






TipTip: Command-line completion





Here are some tips for faster navigation (and fewer typos):

Use the Tab key for autocompletion: type the first few letters of a folder or file name and press Tab. For example, go to your home directory, type cd data_ and press Tab. The shell fills in data_analysis for you.
If there is more than one match, the shell can not decide which one you mean. Press Tab twice to see all options.
Use the ↑ / ↓ arrow keys to scroll through commands you ran before. This is useful to rerun a command or to change a small part of it.

From now on, try to use the Tab key often, so that you do not have to type everything yourself.









QuestionExercise





Get familiar with these first commands:

Create a new folder called results inside your data_analysis folder. We will use it later to store the output of our analyses
Move into the results folder and confirm your location with pwd
Move back into the data_analysis folder
Use ls to confirm that both results and data are there







AnswerClick me to see an answer






# Starting from inside data_analysis
mkdir results
cd results
pwd
cd ..
ls













TipTip: Finding your Desktop and OneDrive folders (optional)





In this tutorial we stay inside the home directory. If you want to work with files that are somewhere else on your computer, for example on your Desktop, these paths help you find them:
Mac

Your Desktop is at /Users/YourUserName/Desktop, or with the ~ shortcut: ~/Desktop

MobaXterm and WSL2 (Windows)
The terminal reaches your Windows files via the C drive, which is found at /mnt/c:

Your Desktop is usually at /mnt/c/Users/YourUserName/Desktop
Or at /mnt/c/Users/YourUserName/OneDrive/Desktop (when using OneDrive)

Accessing the UvA OneDrive folder
If your OneDrive folder name includes spaces (like OneDrive - UvA), put quotes around the path. Otherwise bash does not know what to do with the spaces:

cd "/mnt/c/Users/YourUserName/OneDrive - UvA"

This is also a good example of why you normally do NOT want spaces in your file and folder names.
Be careful with large sequence files in OneDrive folders: OneDrive tries to upload every file you make there.

title: Introduction to Bash
section: Error messages and Ctrl+C: Getting unstuck
text:
Error messages and Ctrl+C: Getting unstuck
Sooner or later, a command will not do what you expect. That is normal, also for people who use the command line every day. Two skills help you get unstuck: reading the error message, and stopping a command.

Reading an error message
Let’s make a mistake on purpose. From inside your data_analysis folder, list a folder with a typo in its name:

# A typo on purpose: the folder is called data, not dta
ls -l dta

This prints something like this:
ls: cannot access 'dta': No such file or directory
An error message is how the shell tells you what went wrong. Read it from left to right:

ls: the command that ran into a problem
cannot access 'dta': what it tried to do, and with which file or folder
No such file or directory: why it did not work

The exact wording can be a bit different on your system, but you find the same three parts.
No such file or directory is the error you will see most often. It usually has one of three causes:

There is a typo in the name. Use the Tab key, so that the shell fills in names for you.
You are in a different folder than you think. Check with pwd and ls.
The file does not exist yet, for example because an earlier step did not work.

If you make a typo in the name of the command itself, for example lss instead of ls, the message contains command not found. The shell does not know a command with that name.
When you ask someone for help, always copy the complete error message. It tells them much more than “it does not work”.


Ctrl+C: Stopping a command
Sometimes a command does not finish, or you start something by mistake. The prompt does not come back, and you can’t type a new command. Press Ctrl+C to stop the command and get your prompt back.
Let’s try it. If you give cat no file name, it waits for you to type text (we use cat for other things later):

# cat without a file name waits for input, so the prompt does not come back
cat

Nothing happens and there is no new prompt. Now press Ctrl+C. The prompt comes back.
Keep in mind that Ctrl+C stops a command, but it does not undo what the command already did.






NotebookNotebook checkpoint: Finding your way





Open notes.md and add:

The mkdir command from the exercise above, which made the results folder, with a comment
One sentence on the difference between an absolute and a relative path

Save the file.






Notebook-answerCompare with my notes





## Setting up the project folder

I made a project folder for this workshop in my home directory.

```bash
# Go to the home directory and make the project folder with a data folder inside
cd ~
mkdir data_analysis
mkdir -p data_analysis/data

# Make the notebook
touch data_analysis/notes.md

# Make a results folder for the output of the analyses
cd data_analysis
mkdir results
```

An absolute path starts at the root `/` and works from anywhere.
A relative path starts from the folder I am in, so it only works from the right place.

title: Introduction to Bash
text:
wget: Download data
Next, let’s download our sequencing data, a file called seq_project.tar.gz, with wget. Make sure that you are inside your data_analysis folder (check with pwd), because wget saves the file in the folder you are currently in:

# Download data using link provided by the sequencing center XYZ on 23.01.2023
wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ndombrowski/cli_workshop/main/data/seq_project.tar.gz

In this example, you can also see how I documented my code: I added where the link came from and when I got it. This helps future me in case I, for example, need to look for some e-mails about the data later on.






ImportantWget for Mac users





For Mac users wget is not installed by default. If you do not want to install it, you can use the curl command instead:

# -L: if the server says that the file is somewhere else, follow it until you reach the actual file
# -O: save the file under its original name
curl -LO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ndombrowski/cli_workshop/main/data/seq_project.tar.gz




After you download any kind of data, it is always a good idea to do a sanity check: is the file there, and how large is it? A file size of 0 means that something went wrong during the download.






QuestionExercise






Check with ls if the file was downloaded correctly
Check the manual if there are extra options that we can use for ls to see the file size in an easy-to-read unit, such as K (kilobytes) or M (megabytes) (advanced)







AnswerClick me to see an answer






# Question 1:
ls -l

# Question 2:
# -h prints the size in a human-readable format
# Options can be combined: -l and -h become -lh
ls -lh

title: Introduction to Bash
text:
cp: Copying data
cp (short for copy) duplicates files or folders. When working with many files, a good folder structure is essential to keep track of them (useful folders are, for example, data, scripts and results). To keep our project folder organized, let’s copy the seq_project.tar.gz file we just downloaded into the data folder we made earlier:

# Copy the tar.gz file into the data folder
cp seq_project.tar.gz data/

# Check what happened
ls -l
ls -l data

When running the two ls commands, we see that we now have two copies of seq_project.tar.gz: one file is in our working directory and the other one is in our data folder. Copying large amounts of data is not ideal, since it uses unnecessary space. However, we can use another command to move the file into our data folder instead.

title: Introduction to Bash
text:
mv: Moving (and renaming) data
mv (short for move) moves files or folders to a new location without creating a second copy:

# Move the tar.gz file into the data folder
mv seq_project.tar.gz data/

# Check what happened
ls -l
ls -l data

Notice that mv moved the file and, without asking, overwrote the copy that we had put into the data folder with cp. So whenever you use mv, make sure that you do not overwrite files by mistake.
mv is also the command to rename a file: you “move” it to a new name, e.g. mv old_name.txt new_name.txt.






TipTip: Downloading directly into a folder (optional)





Instead of downloading a file and moving it afterwards, you can tell wget directly where to save the file with the -P option:

wget -P data https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ndombrowski/cli_workshop/main/data/seq_project.tar.gz

MobaXterm users: MobaXterm comes with a simpler version of wget that does not know the -P option. You see the error wget: Unknown option P. In that case, download the file first and then move it with mv, as we did above.
Mac users: if you use curl instead of wget, you can save the file into a specific folder with --output-dir:

curl --output-dir data -LO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ndombrowski/cli_workshop/main/data/seq_project.tar.gz

title: Introduction to Bash
text:
tar: Work with tar files
The data we downloaded is provided as a tar file:

tar is short for Tape Archive, and sometimes referred to as tarball
The TAR file format is commonly used when storing data
TAR files are often compressed after being created and then become TGZ files, using the tgz, tar.gz, or gz extension.

We can decompress the data into our data folder as follows:

tar -xvf data/seq_project.tar.gz -C data

The options we use with the tar command are:

x tells tar to extract files from the archive
v (verbose) prints the name of each file while it is being extracted, so you can see what happens
f specifies the file name
C tells tar to change directory (so the package content will be unpacked there)







TipTip: How to generate a tarball (optional)





If you ever want to generate a tarball you can do the following:

tar -cvzf my_tarball.tar.gz folder_to_tar

The options we use are:

c create an archive by bundling files and directories together
z use gzip compression when generating the tar file










QuestionExercise






After extracting the tarball, use ls to explore the content of the folder we just extracted. Make sure that you also explore the content of the folders inside it.
Find the path for at least one sequence file that ends with fastq.gz. Hint: use the Tab key (see the tip on command-line completion above), so that you don’t have to type every single word.







AnswerClick me to see an answer






# Question 1:
ls -l data/seq_project

# Question 2:
ls -l data/seq_project/barcode001_User1_ITS_1_L001/

title: Introduction to Bash
text:
rm: Remove files and folders
To remove files and folders, we use the rm command (short for remove). We want to remove the seq_project.tar.gz file, since we do not need it anymore once we have extracted the data:

# Remove the tar.gz file from the data folder
rm data/seq_project.tar.gz

# Check if that worked
ls -l data

If we want to remove a folder, we need to tell rm with an option. For this, we use -r (short for recursive), which removes a folder together with everything inside it.






Important



Unix does not have an undelete command.
This means that if you delete something with rm, it’s gone. There is no recycle bin. Therefore, use rm with care and check what you wrote twice before pressing enter!
Also, NEVER run rm -r or rm -rf on the root folder / or any other important path, such as your home directory. Always double check the path or file name before you press enter when using rm.

title: Introduction to Bash
text:
Wildcards
After we have explored the folder with our sequencing data with ls, we have seen that data/seq_project contains four folders: two folders for two different users who each generated two samples.
You also might have noticed that it gets tedious to figure out how many files are in each folder, because we would need to run ls on each single folder and view its contents one by one. Typing every file name by hand also gets tedious, and you risk typos.
Luckily, the shell provides special characters to work with groups of files using pattern matching. These characters are called wildcards. The most useful wildcard is *, which stands for “any characters, any number of times (also zero times)”. For example, *.txt matches all files that end with .txt.
We can use * to list all files in the seq_project folder as follows:

ls data/seq_project/*


You should have seen before that the sequencing files all end with .fastq.gz. With this, we can make the command a bit more specific and at the same time make the output more readable. */*.gz means “inside any folder, any file that ends with .gz”:

ls data/seq_project/*/*.gz


Now we can easily see for each folder how many files we have.






QuestionExercise






Use a wildcard to list files for barcode001 only
Use a wildcard to only list R1 (forward read) files
Use a wildcard to copy all R1 files into a new folder, call this new folder R1_files. Use ls to confirm if you copied the right files
To avoid duplicates, remove the R1_files folder from question 3 after you have ensured the command you used worked







AnswerClick me to see an answer






# Question 1:
ls data/seq_project/barcode001*/*gz

# Question 2:
ls data/seq_project/*/*R1*

# Question 3:
mkdir R1_files
cp data/seq_project/*/*R1* R1_files
ls data/seq_project/*/*.gz
ls -l R1_files

# Question 4:
rm -r R1_files

After solving question 2 you should see:

After solving question 3, we should see that all files still exist in their original location but are now also inside the R1_files folder. Notice how we can use wildcards together with other commands to easily reorganize our data?












TipTip: More wildcards (optional)





* is not the only wildcard. Square brackets match exactly one character, chosen from a set or a range:

[0-9]: any single digit
[12]: a 1 or a 2
[A-Z]: any single capital letter ([a-z] for a small letter)


# Folders whose name continues with any digit after barcode00
ls data/seq_project/barcode00[0-9]*/*.gz

# Only the folders of barcode001 and barcode002
ls data/seq_project/barcode00[12]*/*.gz

# Any capital letter in front of 001 at the end of the folder name
ls data/seq_project/barcode001_User1_ITS_1_[A-Z]001/*.gz

You find a full list of wildcards here.









TipTip: Finding files with find (optional)





With */*.gz, ls only looks exactly one folder deep inside seq_project. If you don’t know how deep your files are stored, you can use find instead. find searches a folder and all the folders inside it, at any depth:

# Search data/seq_project and all its subfolders for files ending in .gz
find data/seq_project -name "*.gz"


data/seq_project is the folder where find starts searching
-name "*.gz" tells find to only print files whose name ends with .gz

We put quotes around "*.gz" so that the shell passes the * to find unchanged, and find uses it as a pattern while it searches.
If you want to see the full (absolute) path of each file, start the search from your home directory with ~:

find ~/data_analysis/data/seq_project -name "*.gz"

Because the shell replaces ~ with the absolute path to your home directory, find now prints absolute paths, and you don’t need to type your user name. This works on every system.
Note that find does not sort its output alphabetically like ls does, so the files may appear in a different order.

title: Introduction to Bash
text:
I/O redirection to new files
What a command prints is called its standard output. We have seen that by default, commands print their standard output directly to the terminal. For example, when we use ls, the list of files and folders is printed to your terminal. However, we can also redirect the standard output into a file by using the > character.
For example, let’s write a list of all fastq files into a file:

# Write the list of fastq files into a new file instead of to the screen
ls data/seq_project/*/* > fastq_paths.txt

# Check that the new file exists
ls -l fastq_paths.txt

Here:

ls data/seq_project/*/* lists all files in the folders inside seq_project
> tells the shell to write this list into a new file called fastq_paths.txt, instead of printing it to the screen







ImportantImportant: Be careful with >





The > operator overwrites files without asking. If a file with the same name already exists, its content is replaced.
If you want to add (append) to the end of an existing file instead of replacing it, use >>.

title: Introduction to Bash
section: Exploring the content of text files
text:
Exploring the content of text files
Next, let’s look inside the list we just made. Looking at the actual content of your files is one of the best ways to catch mistakes early.

head: View the first lines of a file
head prints the first 10 lines of a file:

# Show the first 10 lines
head fastq_paths.txt



tail: View the last lines of a file
tail prints the last 10 lines:

# Show the last 10 lines
tail fastq_paths.txt

# Show the last 3 lines
# The option -n controls how many lines get printed (this also works for head)
tail -n 3 fastq_paths.txt



less: View the full file
less shows a file one screen at a time. It does not load the whole file at once, so it also opens very large files, such as sequence files, quickly.

less -S fastq_paths.txt

Here:

-S keeps each long line on one line on the screen, instead of continuing it on the next line. Use the → / ← arrow keys to see the rest of a long line
Move up and down with the ↑ / ↓ arrow keys, or with Page Up / Page Down
Press q to quit







TipTip: Editing text files with nano (optional)





You can also change the content of a text file from the command line. The most common tool for this is the text editor nano. It comes with WSL2, Mac and most Linux systems:

nano fastq_paths.txt

Make your changes, and then:

Press Ctrl+X to close the file
Press Y to save the changes, and Enter to keep the file name

MobaXterm users: nano is not installed in MobaXterm by default, and you see nano: command not found. You can install it with apt install nano. Like for wget above, it is only kept after a restart if you chose a permanent folder in MobaXterm.

title: Introduction to Bash
text:
wc: Count things
wc (short for word count) counts the lines, words and characters in a file. With the option -l, it counts only the lines. This is very useful for sanity checks. For example, fastq_paths.txt has one line per fastq file, so counting its lines tells us how many files we work with:

# Count the lines in the file list: one line per fastq file
wc -l fastq_paths.txt

We see that we work with 8 files. Here we could easily count them ourselves, but with hundreds of files, wc -l is much faster and more reliable.
There is one downside: to count the files, we first had to make a file with the list. If we do this for every question we have, we end up with many files that we don’t need. Pipes solve this problem.

title: Introduction to Bash
text:
Pipes
So far, we’ve run one command at a time. But often, you want to combine commands so that the output of one command becomes the input of the next one. That’s what the pipe (|) does. It allows us to chain simple commands together to do more complex things.
Let’s use ls to list all fastq files and then pipe the output from ls into the wc command, to count how many files we work with:

ls data/seq_project/*/* | wc -l

Here:

ls data/seq_project/*/* lists all files in the folders inside seq_project
The pipe (|) sends this list directly to the next command, instead of printing it to the screen
wc -l counts the lines in this list, which is the number of files

Again we see 8 files, but this time without making an extra file first.






QuestionExercise






Use ls and wc to count how many R1 files we have
Count how many R2 files we have
Count how many files were generated for User1







AnswerClick me to see an answer






# Question 1: We see 4 files
ls data/seq_project/*/*R1*gz | wc -l 

# Question 2: We see 4 files
ls data/seq_project/*/*R2*gz | wc -l 

# Question 3: We see 4 files
ls data/seq_project/*_User1_*/*gz | wc -l 

Our data is paired-end sequencing data: each DNA fragment was read from both ends, which gives one R1 file and one R2 file per sample. Having as many R1 as R2 files is a good sanity check: it tells us that we received both files for every sample.

title: Introduction to Bash
section: cut: Extract parts of each line
text:
cut: Extract parts of each line
Each line in fastq_paths.txt is the path to one fastq file, starting from the data_analysis folder. For example you might see this line: data/seq_project/barcode001_User1_ITS_1_L001/Sample-DUMMY1_R1.fastq.gz. What if we only want the file names, without the folders in front of them?
For this, we can use cut, which splits each line into parts and prints only the parts we ask for. We tell cut where to split with a delimiter: a character that separates the parts. In a path, the / is a natural delimiter. Each part between two delimiters is called a field. If we split our example path at each /, we get four fields:

data
seq_project
barcode001_User1_ITS_1_L001
Sample-DUMMY1_R1.fastq.gz

The file name we want is the 4th field and we can then combine this and use cut to extract that information as follows:

# Look at the file list first
head fastq_paths.txt

# Print only the file name: the 4th field when we split at each /
cut -f4 -d "/" fastq_paths.txt

# Do the same, but save the output in a new file
cut -f4 -d "/" fastq_paths.txt > fastq_files.txt

# Check the new file: we expect 8 file names
head fastq_files.txt
wc -l fastq_files.txt

Here:

-d "/": use / as the delimiter
-f4: print the 4th field


We can also chain several cut commands with a pipe. For example, each folder name, such as barcode002_User1_ITS_9_L001, starts with a barcode. To get the barcodes, we first extract the folder name (the 3rd field when we split at /), and then get the first part of the folder name (the 1st field when we split at _):

# Take the folder name (3rd field at /), then the barcode (1st field at _)
cut -f3 -d "/" fastq_paths.txt | cut -f1 -d "_"


This gives us a list of barcodes. But note how each barcode appears twice: once for the R1 file and once for the R2 file. If we want to make a table with information about each sample, we need each barcode only once. For that, we need to learn about two more commands.

title: Introduction to Bash
section: sort and uniq: Create unique lists
text:
sort and uniq: Create unique lists

sort sorts lines from A to Z
uniq removes duplicate lines, but only when they are directly below each other. That is why we almost always use sort before uniq: sorting puts identical lines next to each other


# Extract the barcodes, sorted, with each barcode appearing only once
cut -f3 -d "/" fastq_paths.txt | cut -f1 -d "_" | sort | uniq

# Question 2:

# Question 3:

title: Introduction to Bash
text:
cat: Read and combine files
cat is short for concatenate, which means “link together”. We use it for two things:

Print the content of a file to the screen
Combine several files into one. You give cat the files one after the other, or use a wildcard

To print a file:

# Print the whole file to the screen
cat fastq_paths.txt

Unlike less, cat prints the whole file at once. So only use it for short files.
To combine files:

# Make a folder for the combined files inside results
mkdir -p results/combined

# Combine two files into one
cat fastq_paths.txt fastq_files.txt > results/combined/combined_files.txt

# View the new file
cat results/combined/combined_files.txt

Notice how we keep the output in its own subfolder of results? Giving each analysis its own folder inside results keeps the project folder clean, and later you can see right away which files belong together.






QuestionExercise





You can also combine fastq.gz files with cat. We don’t need this for our data, but you might need it for your own. For example, a sequencing center sometimes sends several files for one sample, because the data is too large for a single file.

Use a wildcard and cat to combine all R1 fastq.gz files into one file called combined_R1.fastq.gz, in the results/combined folder
Use ls to compare the size of the individual R1 files with the size of the combined file. Did it work?







AnswerClick me to see an answer






# Question 1:
cat data/seq_project/*/*R1.fastq.gz > results/combined/combined_R1.fastq.gz

# Question 2:
ls -lh data/seq_project/*/*R1.fastq.gz
ls -lh results/combined/combined_R1.fastq.gz

The combined file should be about as large as all the individual R1 files together.

title: Introduction to Bash
section: Exploring the content of compressed fastq files
text:
Exploring the content of compressed fastq files






QuestionExercise






Use head to view the first lines of one of the fastq.gz files
Does this look like sequence data to you?







AnswerClick me to see an answer






head data/seq_project/barcode001_User1_ITS_1_L001/Sample-DUMMY1_R1.fastq.gz

You see a lot of strange characters, but nothing that looks like a DNA sequence. What is going on?







gzip: (De)compress files
You might have noticed that our sequence files end with .gz. This extension is used for files that are compressed with a tool called gzip. Compressing makes a file smaller, which saves space, but it also makes the file unreadable for a human. That is why head showed us random characters.
To view the content of a compressed file, we can decompress it first. We do this with the gzip command together with the -d (decompress) option. Without -d, gzip compresses a file.
gzip -d replaces the compressed file with the decompressed one. We never want to change our raw data in data/: if something goes wrong, there is no way to get the original back. So we instead make us of a copy:

# Make a folder for this test, so that the raw data in data/ stays as it is
mkdir -p results/gzip_test

# Copy one sequence file into it
cp data/seq_project/barcode001_User1_ITS_1_L001/Sample-DUMMY1_R1.fastq.gz results/gzip_test/

# Decompress the copy
gzip -d results/gzip_test/Sample-DUMMY1_R1.fastq.gz

# Check that this worked: the file lost its .gz extension
ls -l results/gzip_test

# View the first lines of the decompressed file
head results/gzip_test/Sample-DUMMY1_R1.fastq

Now we finally see DNA sequences, plus some other information. Each sequence that the sequencer read from a DNA fragment is called a read. In a fastq file, every read always takes 4 lines:









QuestionExercise






Use ls with an option to view the file size in an easy-to-read unit (remember the wget exercise)
Compare the size of the decompressed copy in results/gzip_test with the compressed original in data/







AnswerClick me to see an answer






# The compressed original
ls -lh data/seq_project/barcode001_User1_ITS_1_L001/Sample-DUMMY1_R1.fastq.gz

# The decompressed copy
ls -lh results/gzip_test/Sample-DUMMY1_R1.fastq

We see that the decompressed file has a size of about ~25M, while the compressed file is around ~5M.
Real sequencing data is usually much larger, so it is best to keep the files compressed.






To compress a file again, use gzip without -d:

# Compress the copy again: it gets its .gz extension back
gzip results/gzip_test/Sample-DUMMY1_R1.fastq

# Check that this worked
ls -l results/gzip_test

We don’t need the test folder anymore, so we remove it. Check the path twice before you press Enter, rm -r does not ask:

# Remove the test folder and everything inside it
rm -r results/gzip_test

# Check that it is gone
ls results



zcat: Decompress and print to screen
Decompressing a file to look at it works, but it takes extra space and changes the file. zcat is a better way: it decompresses the file and prints the content to the screen, but leaves the compressed file as it is. We combine it with head, because we only want to see the first lines, not millions of reads:

# Print the first 10 lines of a compressed file, without changing the file
zcat data/seq_project/barcode001_User1_ITS_1_L001/Sample-DUMMY1_R1.fastq.gz | head







Importantzcat for Mac users





On a Mac, zcat might not work as expected. Try gzcat instead:

gzcat data/seq_project/barcode001_User1_ITS_1_L001/Sample-DUMMY1_R1.fastq.gz | head

title: Introduction to Bash
text:
grep: Find patterns in data
grep searches a file for lines that contain a word or a pattern (a piece of text you search for), and prints these lines. It is simple, but very useful for sanity checks.
The basic form is grep "pattern" file. We put quotes around the pattern, so that special characters, such as > or spaces, are passed on to grep safely.
For example, to print only the lines for the R1 files:

# Print all lines in fastq_paths.txt that contain R1
grep "R1" fastq_paths.txt

If you only want to know how many lines match, add the option -c (count):

# Count the lines in fastq_paths.txt that contain R1
grep -c "R1" fastq_paths.txt

To look only at the samples from User1, we search for that part of the path:

# Print all lines in fastq_paths.txt that contain User1
grep "User1" fastq_paths.txt







QuestionExercise






Use grep to print the paths in fastq_paths.txt that contain the pattern “ITS_9”
Search for the pattern “AAGACG” in one of the fastq.gz files (advanced)
Count how many lines in that file contain “AAGACG” (advanced)







AnswerClick me to see an answer






# Question 1
grep "ITS_9" fastq_paths.txt

# Question 2
zcat data/seq_project/barcode001_User1_ITS_1_L001/Sample-DUMMY1_R1.fastq.gz | grep "AAGACG"

# Question 3
zcat data/seq_project/barcode001_User1_ITS_1_L001/Sample-DUMMY1_R1.fastq.gz | grep -c "AAGACG"

For questions 2 and 3, grep can’t read the compressed file directly, so we send the output of zcat to it with a pipe. Commands like these are useful to check whether adapters or primers are still part of your reads. These are short, known DNA sequences that are added to or used on the DNA before sequencing.

title: Introduction to Bash
text:
wc: Count things II
wc -l also works on the output of zcat. Since every read takes 4 lines, this tells us how many reads a fastq file has:

# Count the lines in one compressed fastq file
zcat data/seq_project/barcode001_User1_ITS_1_L001/Sample-DUMMY1_R2.fastq.gz | wc -l

For Sample-DUMMY1_R2.fastq.gz, this gives 179,384 lines. Every read takes 4 lines, so the file has 179,384 / 4 = 44,846 reads.






TipTip: Better counting (optional)





Dividing by 4 with a calculator works, but bash can also do it for us:

zcat data/seq_project/barcode001_User1_ITS_1_L001/Sample-DUMMY1_R2.fastq.gz | echo $(( $(wc -l) /4))

Here:

$( ) is called command substitution. Bash runs the command inside the brackets, here wc -l, and puts its output in its place. wc -l counts the lines that zcat sends through the pipe
$(( )) is called arithmetic expansion. Bash calculates what is inside the double brackets, here the number of lines divided by 4, and puts the result in its place
echo prints the result

title: Introduction to Bash
text:
echo and variables: Storing information
Next, we learn how we can use the command line to automate repetitive tasks. But first, we need to learn about two small building blocks.
The first one is echo. It prints the text you give it to the screen:

echo "Hello"

The second one is a variable. A variable is a name that stores a value, for example a word, a number or a file path. You create a variable by writing its name, an equals sign and the value:

# Store the path to one sequencing file in a variable called fastq_file
fastq_file=data/seq_project/barcode001_User1_ITS_1_L001/Sample-DUMMY1_R1.fastq.gz

This prints nothing, however Bash will remember the value. To use the value, put a $ in front of the variable name. Bash then replaces $fastq_file with the path we stored:

# Print the value stored in the variable
echo $fastq_file

# Use the variable in a command, exactly like you would use the path itself
zcat $fastq_file | wc -l

The second command gives the same result as typing out the full path. On its own, that does not save us much work. Variables become really useful when their value changes, and that is exactly what a for-loop does for us in the next section.
A few rules for variables:

The name can contain letters, numbers and underscores (_), but no spaces. Choose a name that tells you what is stored in it, fastq_file is easier to understand a year later than x.
A variable only exists in the terminal window where you made it. If you close the terminal, it is gone.







ImportantImportant: No spaces around =





Write fastq_file=data/... without spaces around the =. If you add spaces (fastq_file = data/...), bash thinks that fastq_file is the name of a command, and you get an error that ends with fastq_file: command not found.

title: Introduction to Bash
text:
For-loops
Imagine we want to count the lines not only in one, but in all files. Could we do something like the code below?

zcat data/seq_project/*/*.fastq.gz | wc -l

When running this, we see that the command prints a single number, 869 944, but not the counts for each individual file, so something did not work right.
The problem with this command is that it prints the text from all 8 fastq files and only afterwards counts the lines. We basically combined all files and then counted the lines of all 8 files together. However, what we want is to repeat the steps below, individually for each file:

Decompress a first file
Count the lines in the first file
Decompress a second file
Count the lines in the second file
…

A for-loop repeats one or more commands, once for each item in a list. Each round of the loop is called an iteration.

Step 1: Check what the loop works on
Let’s write a first loop that does not change anything yet. It only prints the names of our sequencing files:

for fastq_file in data/seq_project/*/*.fastq.gz; do
    echo $fastq_file
done

This prints the paths of all 8 fastq files, one per line. Let’s go through the parts of the loop:

for fastq_file in data/seq_project/*/*.fastq.gz; do: this line says what to repeat over. The wildcard gives the list, here all 8 fastq files. In each iteration, bash stores the next file from the list in the variable fastq_file. You choose the name of this variable yourself.
echo $fastq_file: the command we want to repeat, written between do and done. Here, we print the value of the variable. We indent this line with 4 spaces. Bash does not need this, but it makes the loop easier to read.
done: marks the end of the loop.

In other words, the loop does the same as typing these commands one after the other:

# You don't need to run this, it only shows what the loop does for us
fastq_file=data/seq_project/barcode001_User1_ITS_1_L001/Sample-DUMMY1_R1.fastq.gz
echo $fastq_file
fastq_file=data/seq_project/barcode001_User1_ITS_1_L001/Sample-DUMMY1_R2.fastq.gz
echo $fastq_file
# ... and so on, for the other 6 files

Starting a loop with echo is a good habit. This is called a dry run: the loop shows what it would work on, without changing anything. Before you add the real command, check the list. Do you see all 8 files, and only the files you expect? If yes, then you can continue with the next step and build up the loop for more complex tasks.






TipTip: Typing a loop in the terminal





When you press Enter after writing the first line of the loop, nothing runs yet. Instead, the prompt changes to >. This means bash waits for the rest of the loop. It only starts once you type done and press Enter. (On a Mac with zsh, this prompt may look slightly different, for example for>.)
If you get stuck in this > prompt, for example because of a typo, press Ctrl+C to cancel and start again.





Step 2: Add the real command
Now that we know the loop works on the right files, we can replace echo with the command we actually want to run:

for fastq_file in data/seq_project/*/*.fastq.gz; do
    zcat $fastq_file | wc -l
done

Now we get 8 numbers, one per file. zcat $fastq_file | wc -l is the same command as in the variables section. The only difference is that bash now runs it 8 times, each time with a different file stored in fastq_file.






TipTip: Loops written on one line (optional)





You might also see loops written on a single line, with ; where we start a new line:

for fastq_file in data/seq_project/*/*.fastq.gz; do zcat $fastq_file | wc -l; done

This does exactly the same as the loop above. For anything longer than one short command, the version over several lines is easier to read.









QuestionExercise






Use a for-loop and count how often grep finds the pattern “TAAGA” in each individual fastq.gz file







AnswerClick me to see an answer






for fastq_file in data/seq_project/*/*.fastq.gz; do
    zcat $fastq_file | grep -c "TAAGA"
done

title: Introduction to Bash
section: >>: Collecting the loop output in one file
text:
>>: Collecting the loop output in one file
So far, the counts only appear on the screen. We cannot see which number belongs to which file, and the numbers are gone once we close the terminal. Let’s write the file names and the counts into a file instead.
In the section on I/O redirection, we have seen that > replaces the content of a file, and that >> adds (appends) text to the end of a file. Inside a loop, this difference matters. With >, each iteration would replace what the iteration before it wrote, and only the result for the last file would be left. So inside the loop we use >>:

# Make a folder for the counts inside results
mkdir -p results/counts

# Start the counts file with a first line that describes its content
# Because we use > here, an existing file is emptied first, so we start fresh each time
echo "Number of lines per fastq file" > results/counts/line_counts.txt

# For each fastq file, add the file name and its number of lines to the end of the file
for fastq_file in data/seq_project/*/*.fastq.gz; do
    echo $fastq_file >> results/counts/line_counts.txt
    zcat $fastq_file | wc -l >> results/counts/line_counts.txt
done

# Check the result: we expect 1 header line + 2 lines for each of the 8 files = 17 lines
wc -l results/counts/line_counts.txt
cat results/counts/line_counts.txt

Here:

mkdir -p results/counts: we keep the output of each analysis in its own folder inside results
echo "Number of lines per fastq file" > results/counts/line_counts.txt: before the loop starts, we write a first line that describes what is in the file. Such a line is called a header. Because we use > here, this also empties the file if it already exists from an earlier run
Inside the loop, there are now two commands. The first one adds the name of the file, the second one adds its number of lines. Both use >>, so each iteration adds two lines to the end of line_counts.txt

We will use these numbers again on day 2, to check what a quality filtering tool did to our data.






QuestionExercise






Run only the for-loop from the code above a second time, without the echo line before it. How many lines does line_counts.txt have now? Why?
Now run the complete code again, including the echo line before the loop. How many lines does line_counts.txt have now?
What do you think would happen if we used > instead of >> inside the loop? Think about it first, then try it. Afterwards, run the code with >> once more, so that line_counts.txt is correct again.







AnswerClick me to see an answer






The file now has 33 lines. The loop added its 16 lines a second time to the end of the file, so all counts appear twice. This is something to watch out for whenever you use >>.
The file has 17 lines again. The echo line uses >, which empties the file before the loop adds the counts.
Each > replaces the content of the file. After the loop, the file only contains a single line: the number of lines of the last file. All other results were overwritten.













TipTip: Better counting in for loops (optional)





In our counts file, each file name and its count end up on two separate lines. With 100 files, it is much easier to read if the file name and its count are on the same line. We can do this with the command substitution from the tip “Better counting” in the section “wc: Count things II”:

for fastq_file in data/seq_project/*/*.fastq.gz; do
    echo "$fastq_file: $(zcat $fastq_file | wc -l)"
done

Here:

echo "..." prints the text between the double quotes. Inside double quotes, bash still replaces $fastq_file with the file name, and $( ) with the output of the command inside it
So for each file, echo prints the file name, a colon, a space and the number of lines

To get the number of reads, we also divide by 4 with the arithmetic expansion $(( )):

for fastq_file in data/seq_project/*/*.fastq.gz; do
    echo "$fastq_file: $(( $(zcat $fastq_file | wc -l) /4 ))"
done

Notice the single and the double brackets: $( ) runs a command, $(( )) calculates.









TipTip: Using bash to make sample mapping files (optional)





Many tools for amplicon analysis need a table that lists your files, often with the R1 and the R2 file of each sample in separate columns. This is called a sample mapping file. Let’s have a look at how we could automatically make one with bash.
The code below uses a few things we have not covered. We won’t go into every detail but the goal is to show you what is possible with bash.

for file in data/seq_project/*/*.gz; do
    if [[ $file == *_R1.fastq.gz ]]; then
        r1_file=$file
        r2_file=$(echo $file | sed 's/_R1/_R2/')
        echo "$r1_file,$r2_file"
    fi
done

Here:

for file in data/seq_project/*/*.gz: loop over all fastq.gz files
if [[ $file == *_R1.fastq.gz ]]; then … fi: run the lines between then and fi only if the file name ends in _R1.fastq.gz. So the loop skips the R2 files
r1_file=$file: store the path of the R1 file in the variable r1_file
r2_file=$(echo $file | sed 's/_R1/_R2/'): the command sed replaces _R1 with _R2 in the path. This gives the path of the matching R2 file, which we store in the variable r2_file
echo "$r1_file,$r2_file": print both paths on one line, separated by a comma

We can add a column with the name of the sample folder, with cut from above:

for file in data/seq_project/*/*.gz; do
    if [[ $file == *_R1.fastq.gz ]]; then
        sample_name=$(echo $file | cut -f3 -d "/" )
        r1_file=$file
        r2_file=$(echo $file | sed 's/_R1/_R2/')
        echo "$sample_name,$r1_file,$r2_file"
    fi
done

Or, with a second cut, we could only add the barcode:

for file in data/seq_project/*/*.gz; do
    if [[ $file == *_R1.fastq.gz ]]; then
        sample_name=$(echo $file | cut -f3 -d "/"  |cut -f1 -d "_" )
        r1_file=$file
        r2_file=$(echo $file | sed 's/_R1/_R2/')
        echo "$sample_name,$r1_file,$r2_file"
    fi
done

title: Introduction to Bash
section: bash: Running commands from a script
text:
bash: Running commands from a script
Our counting loop is now a few lines long, and we might want to run it again later, for example when new data arrives. Instead of typing or copying the loop each time, we can save it in a file. A text file that contains commands is called a script. Bash scripts usually end with .sh.
To keep our project folder tidy, we store scripts in their own folder:

# Make a folder for scripts inside data_analysis
mkdir -p scripts

# Check that the folder was created
ls -l

Next, we create the script with the text editor nano (see the tip “Editing text files with nano” above):

nano scripts/count_lines.sh

MobaXterm users: if you see nano: command not found, install it first with apt install nano, as explained in that tip.
Type or copy the following into the editor:

#!/bin/bash

# Count the number of lines in each fastq file
# Run this script from inside the data_analysis folder

# Make a folder for the counts and start the counts file with a header
mkdir -p results/counts
echo "Number of lines per fastq file" > results/counts/line_counts_bash.txt

# For each fastq file, add the file name and its number of lines to the end of the file
for fastq_file in data/seq_project/*/*.fastq.gz; do
    echo $fastq_file >> results/counts/line_counts_bash.txt
    zcat $fastq_file | wc -l >> results/counts/line_counts_bash.txt
done

Save and exit:

Press Ctrl+X to exit, then Y to confirm that you want to save the file, then Enter to keep the file name

The commands are the same as in the >> section. Two things are new:

#!/bin/bash: this first line is called the shebang. It tells the system that the script should be run with bash. Put it at the very top of every bash script.
The lines that start with # are comments. Bash ignores them, but they tell you (and others) what the script does and how to use it.

Now we can run the whole script with a single command:

# Run the script with bash
bash scripts/count_lines.sh

# Check the output: we again expect 17 lines
wc -l results/counts/line_counts_bash.txt
cat results/counts/line_counts_bash.txt

The script itself prints nothing to the screen, because all output goes into line_counts_bash.txt. That is why we check the file afterwards.
Why is this useful?

You can run the same analysis again, with exactly the same commands, without typing mistakes.
The script documents what you did. Together with your notebook (notes.md), it tells future you how a result was made.
On day 2, we use exactly this kind of script on the HPC. There, we add a few extra lines at the top that tell the HPC how many resources our job needs.







ImportantImportant: Write scripts in nano or a code editor, not in Word or Notepad





Windows programs such as Notepad end every line with an extra invisible character. Bash on Linux does not understand this character, and the script fails with errors such as $'\r': command not found or syntax error near unexpected token. Word processors such as Word also add formatting and can change straight quotes (") into curly quotes.
To avoid this, write your scripts with nano. If you prefer a code editor such as VS Code, check that it saves the file with LF line endings (in VS Code, you see LF or CRLF in the bar at the bottom right, and can click it to change it). This becomes important on day 2, where the scripts run on a Linux computer.









NotebookNotebook checkpoint: Counting lines per file





Add a new heading ## Counting lines per file to notes.md, and below it:

The command that ran the script, with a comment that says what the script does and which file it makes. We use results/counts/line_counts_bash.txt again on day 2
The check you ran afterwards, and below the code block, what you expected and what you saw

You don’t need to copy the loop itself into your notebook, because it is saved in scripts/count_lines.sh. The script is part of your documentation. Your notebook only needs to say which script you ran and what it made.

text:
Description
The goal of this workflow is to analyse sequencing data received on 23.01.2023 from Data Science Sequencing Centre. text:
Software
All analyses were run on the UvA Crunchomics HPC with a CentOS 7 operating system.
Dependencies:

SeqKit v2.7.0 (pre-installed)
fastp v1.4.0 (conda environment fastp_1.4.0)

mamba create -n fastp_1.4.0 -c bioconda fastp=1.4.0

title: My report for analysis X (project title)
text:
Analysis workflow

Settings (change these before you run the workflow)

# Path to working directory
wdir="$HOME/personal/data_analysis"

# Custom variables
download_link="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ndombrowski/cli_workshop/main/data/seq_project.tar.gz"



Getting the data

# Go to project dir
cd $wdir 

# Setup base folders
mkdir data scripts logs results

# Download data using link provided by the sequencing center on 23.01.2023
wget -P data $download_link
tar -xvf data/seq_project.tar.gz -C data
rm data/*.tar.gz

# Generate a list for the files we work with 
ls data/seq_project/*/*.gz | cut -f4 -d "/" > fastq_files.txt

# Generate a list of sample names (used in scripts/fastp.sh)
ls data/seq_project/*/*_R1.fastq.gz | cut -f4 -d "/" | cut -f1 -d "_" > samples.txt



Looking at the data

# We work with 8 files from 4 samples
wc -l fastq_files.txt
wc -l samples.txt

# We have as many R1 as we have R2 files
ls data/seq_project/*/*R1* | wc -l
ls data/seq_project/*/*R2* | wc -l

# The sequence header looks as expected
zcat data/seq_project/*/*gz | head

# R1 and R2 reads have the same number of reads
mkdir -p results/counts

for fastq_file in $(cat fastq_files.txt); do
    echo "$fastq_file: $(( $(zcat data/seq_project/*/$fastq_file | wc -l) /4 ))"
done > results/counts/read_counts.txt

# We expect 8 lines, one per fastq file
wc -l results/counts/read_counts.txt
cat results/counts/read_counts.txt

We work with so many reads per fastq file:
Sample-DUMMY1_R1.fastq.gz: 44846
Sample-DUMMY1_R2.fastq.gz: 44846
Sample-DUMMY2_R1.fastq.gz: 19733
Sample-DUMMY2_R2.fastq.gz: 19733
Sample-DUMMY3_R1.fastq.gz: 19784
Sample-DUMMY3_R2.fastq.gz: 19784
Sample-DUMMY4_R1.fastq.gz: 24380
Sample-DUMMY4_R2.fastq.gz: 24380


Read statistics with seqkit

Run seqkit stats

mkdir -p results/seqkit

# Submitted batch job 380625
sbatch scripts/seqkit.sh

# We expect one table with a header line and one line per fastq file (9 lines)
ls -l results/seqkit
wc -l results/seqkit/stats_raw.txt
cat results/seqkit/stats_raw.txt

# Get some basic summary statistics with awk:
# -F'\t': the columns in the table are separated by tabs
# NR>1: skip the first line (the header)
# reads+=$4; bp+=$5: add up column 4 (num_seqs) and column 5 (sum_len); n++ counts the files
# END {...}: after the last line, print the totals and the mean per fastq file
awk -F'\t' 'NR>1 {reads+=$4; bp+=$5; n++}
    END {print "files:", n; print "reads:", reads; print "bp:", bp; printf "mean reads per file: %.1f\n", reads/n; printf "mean bp per file: %.1f\n", bp/n}' results/seqkit/stats_raw.txt

Comments on the read statistics from seqkit stats:

We work with a total of

217,486 reads (avg 27,186 read pairs per sample)
54,493,987 bp (avg 6,811,748 bp per fastq file)

The number of reads (num_seqs) matches the read counts from the sanity checks above, and R1 and R2 have the same number of reads for each sample
The reads are typically 251 bp long (the average length is 250-251 bp), but each file also contains some shorter reads (shortest read: 35-239 bp). This suggests that there was some pre-trimming done by the sequencing center
The R1 reads have a higher quality than the R2 reads: 94-95% of the bases in R1 have a quality score of at least 30 (Q30(%)), compared to 89-90% in R2
The GC content is 53-57%




Quality filtering with fastp

Run fastp

mkdir -p results/fastp

# Submitted batch job 380626
sbatch scripts/fastp.sh

# We expect 4 samples x 4 files (2 trimmed fastq.gz, 1 html, 1 json) = 16 files
ls results/fastp | wc -l



Run seqkit stats on the trimmed reads

# Submitted batch job 380627
sbatch scripts/seqkit_trimmed.sh

# We expect one table with a header line and one line per trimmed fastq file (9 lines)
ls -l results/seqkit
wc -l results/seqkit/stats_trimmed.txt

# Same summary statistics as for the raw reads
awk -F'\t' 'NR>1 {reads+=$4; bp+=$5; n++}
    END {print "files:", n; print "reads:", reads; print "bp:", bp; printf "mean reads per file: %.1f\n", reads/n; printf "mean bp per file: %.1f\n", bp/n}' results/seqkit/stats_trimmed.txt

Comments on the seqkit output post trimming:

After cleaning we work with

214,906 out of 217,486 reads (98.8% maintained)
53,826,288 out of 54,493,987 bp (98.8% maintained)

Information from the fastp html:

Little adapter sequence signal (< 0.05%)
Read quality drops at the beginning and end of the read –> reconsider re-running fastp and use --cut_front, --cut_front_window_size 4 (default setting) and --cut_front_mean_quality 20 (default setting). Note that --cut_front is disabled by default
