title: Introduction to the cli
text:
Welcome page
On this website, you find a short tutorial that teaches you how to use the command line with bash, and how to connect to and work on an HPC.
On the first page, you set up a terminal. Then the actual tutorial begins. In it, you take the role of a researcher who received data from a sequencing center, and who wants to start analysing this data on the command line. While you work, you keep a notebook in which you document what you did and why. The tutorial has two main parts:

In the first part, you will use bash on your own computer: you learn how to organize your data, look at it and extract information from it
In the second part, you learn how to work with your data on an HPC: you learn how to connect to the HPC, copy your sequencing data to it, install software and run jobs that check and clean your sequencing data

I wrote this tutorial for researchers at the Institute for Biodiversity and Ecosystem Dynamics (IBED) at the University of Amsterdam, who can get access to Crunchomics, the Genomics Compute Environment for SILS and IBED. If you don’t have access to Crunchomics or another HPC that uses SLURM, you can still follow most of the tutorial on your own computer.
For topics that this tutorial does not cover, have a look at IBED’s bioinformatics guidance page.

title: Introduction to the cli
text:
An example notebook
If you want to see an example of documented code, have a look at a notebook that I wrote for the analysis we do in this tutorial. You can think of it as a cleaned-up version of the notes.md notebook that you kept during the workshop.
The link above shows you:

How you can use GitHub to make your code available to others
How you can organize a project folder, with a README.md file that explains what is in the folder and where to start
What a code notebook can look like. The notebook is a Quarto file, which you find here. To make it easier to read for collaborators, I also turned it into an HTML report.

In the example, the notebook has its own folder, notebook/, next to the scripts/ folder. In the tutorial, you kept your notes.md directly in data_analysis/. Both work. A separate folder keeps a bigger project tidy, but all commands still run from the project folder itself.
The example uses the same data as this tutorial, so the code might only make sense after you have finished the tutorial. Feel free to come back to this page after you have written some code yourself.
This is just one example to get you started. Your own notebook might look different, depending on your needs.
Below, you find some hints on what to put into the different sections of the notebook.

YAML headers

The YAML header is the part between the two --- lines at the very top of the file. It contains settings for the whole document, such as the title, the author and the output format. In my example, eval: false tells Quarto to only show the code, not to run it.


Settings (change these before you run the workflow)

In one of the first sections of my notebooks, I collect everything that someone who wants to use my workflow has to change. I write the code below this section in a way that it does not need to be changed. This way, another person can run my code as it is, and only needs to edit this first section. Typical things to add here are:

Where the analysis starts: the location of the working directory or project folder
Custom paths, for example to databases that need to be downloaded from the web
Custom variables. In the example above, I store the location of my project folder in a variable called wdir. I use $HOME in it instead of typing out my home directory, so the path works for anyone with the same folder structure on Crunchomics. I also store the link to the data in a variable called download_link, and use this variable further down to download the data. If the link to the data ever changes, another person only needs to change it in this one place, and the code below stays the same. When you write code, try to think ahead: keep the number of places that need to be changed as small as possible.

I tend NOT to write down how I log in to the HPC with ssh and copy data with scp. That way, my user name and login information stay private.


Looking at the data (sanity checks)

When I start working with new data, I add as many sanity checks as possible, to make sure that my data looks good. That way, I notice problems early, before they cause trouble further down the line. At the same time, I get to know my data better: how many samples and how much data I am working with.
I also add sanity checks whenever I change my data. For example, when I merge several files into one large file, I might count the lines of the individual files and of the combined file, to make sure that I used my wildcards correctly.
Remember: the computer is only as smart as the person using it, and it runs your commands blindly. So the computer can do unexpected things, and you need to check for that.


Using Markdown to make notes

In the example above, I use Markdown not only to document my code, but also to add notes wherever I need them. Here, I wrote down what the results of seqkit stats and the fastp HTML reports actually told me.
This kind of documentation can be useful for:

Justifying decisions further down the line. In this example, I might decide on how to clean the sequencing data. For example, when I looked at the FastP HTML report I noticed a dip in quality at the end of the sequence reads. Based on that I normally would make a decision to adjust re-run FastP and enable trimming of the reads.
Future you. If you read the report a month, or a year, later you have the key information in your report and don’t have to open any files or tables that are located elsewhere



Documenting external scripts

This part makes more sense after you have worked through the HPC part of the tutorial. Here, my notebook only says that I submitted a script to the HPC with sbatch. It does not say how I ran seqkit: that code is “hidden” inside the seqkit.sh script. So someone who reads only the notebook does not see the code right away. You can deal with this in two ways:

Instead of the sbatch command, write the actual command that ran on the compute node into your notebook.
Keep the scripts next to your notebook, and when you publish your code with a paper, publish the whole scripts folder too, for example on GitHub or Zenodo. This is why you copied the job scripts to your own computer at the end of day 2.

I prefer option 2, because I like to record the code in my notebooks exactly as I ran it. But you can do it differently, as long as all the code you ran is written down and available to others once you publish your data.

title: Introduction to the cli
text:
Going further

From notes.md to a Quarto document
Your notes.md and my example notebook are written in the same way: Markdown text with code blocks. The difference is that the example notebook is a Quarto document (it ends in .qmd). Quarto turns such a file into a web page (HTML), a PDF or a Word file, with a table of contents and colored code. That makes it easier to share your notebook with others, for example with your supervisor or together with a paper.
If you want to try this in RStudio (recent versions of RStudio come with Quarto):

Go to File, then New File, then Quarto Document
Copy the content of your notes.md into the new file, below the YAML header at the top (see “YAML headers” above)
Save the file and click Render

Code blocks that you wrote as ```bash, like in your notes, are only shown on the page, not run. The Quarto tutorial for RStudio explains the next steps.


Further reading

A Guide to Reproducible Code in Ecology and Evolution from the British Ecological Society explains how to organize project folders and how to write clear code that others can rerun. The examples are mostly in R, but the advice applies to bash and other languages as well.
Markdown Basics on the Quarto website lists everything else you can do with Markdown, for example lists, links, bold text, images and tables.

title: Introduction to the cli
text:
HPC introduction
On day 2, we work on Crunchomics, the Genomics Compute Environment for SILS and IBED. Crunchomics is an HPC (high-performance computer): a group of powerful computers that many people share. If you work at IBED, you can get access to it by sending an email with your UvAnetID to Wim de Leeuw (w.c.deleeuw@uva.nl), as described on the Before you start page.
Working on an HPC is a bit different from working on your own computer. The figure below gives a simplified overview:






When you log in, you arrive on the login node, also called the head node. This computer is for preparing your work, for example moving and editing files and writing job scripts. It is not for running analyses.
The analyses run on the compute nodes. These computers have many more CPUs and much more memory.
In between is SLURM, a workload manager (also called a scheduler) that is used on many large HPCs. You send your analysis to SLURM as a job, and SLURM runs it on a compute node. SLURM does three things:

It gives users access to CPUs and memory on the compute nodes, for a limited time
It starts and runs the jobs, and lets you check on them
It manages the queue: the list of jobs that wait until enough CPUs and memory are free








Important



Crunchomics etiquette
You share Crunchomics with many other people, so only ask for the resources that you actually use. There are no hard limits, but please follow these rules:

Do NOT run jobs that need many CPUs or a lot of memory on the login node (omics-h0). Use the compute nodes (omics-cn001 to omics-cn005) for this
Do NOT use more than 20% of the CPUs or memory of the cluster for more than a day. If you have large jobs, contact Wim de Leeuw
Don’t leave resources that you reserved unused, and set reasonable time limits on your jobs
Use the queue (SLURM) for large jobs. Working interactively is possible, but not for large jobs. We learn how to use the queue on day 2
Close programs when you don’t use them anymore, for example an R session

title: Introduction to the cli
text:
Storage
On Crunchomics, you have two folders ($USER stands for your user name):

Your home directory, /home/$USER, with 25 GB of space
Your personal directory, /zfs/omics/personal/$USER, with 500 GB of space. On day 2, we make a shortcut to it, ~/personal, and keep our project folder there

Good to know:

Your data is removed from Crunchomics when your UvAnetID expires
If you need more space, or a shared folder for a larger project with several team members, contact the Crunchomics team
Snapshots: every day at midnight (00:00), Crunchomics makes a snapshot, a saved copy of your files, and keeps it for 2 weeks. So if you delete a file by mistake, it can be restored for up to 2 weeks. But this also means that files you delete still count towards your storage limit for 2 weeks
Your data is stored on several disks, which protects it if one disk breaks. But it is not copied anywhere else. Crunchomics is not a backup or an archive. You are responsible for backing up your own data. The website of the IBED computational support team explains the archiving options at the UvA
